items.b_text: Methodological and sample characteristics serve as moderators of relationships between cyberbullying and behavioral/psychological variables.
items.explanation: Claim B's finding that methodological and sample characteristics act as moderators helps explain and reinforce the inconsistent correlations between cyberbullying and anxiety noted in Claim A.

items.a_text: An RBF Support Vector Machine classifier using dimension-reduced social media and demographic features achieves 70.35% positive class accuracy and 0.742 precision in predicting depression ahead of onset.
items.b_text: Predictive markers of depression are detectable in Instagram posts made prior to the date of first clinical diagnosis.
items.explanation: Both claims independently demonstrate that social media data contains detectable predictive markers capable of forecasting depression prior to its formal onset or diagnosis.

items.a_text: Adolescents who spent more time on new media were more likely to report mental health issues.
items.b_text: Adolescents aged 14 to 17 with high screen use (7+ hours per day vs 1 hour per day) are more than twice as likely to have taken medication for a psychological or behavioral issue in the last 12 months (RR 2.99).
items.explanation: Both claims independently indicate that higher screen or new media use among adolescents is associated with an increased likelihood of mental health issues or related interventions.

items.a_text: The positive well-being effects of taking a break from Facebook are significantly greater for users who tend to envy others on Facebook.
items.b_text: Overall, the use of Facebook is negatively associated with well-being.
items.explanation: The finding that taking a break from Facebook improves well-being reinforces the finding that Facebook use is negatively associated with well-being.

items.a_text: Loneliness predicts subsequent increases in Facebook usage over time.
items.b_text: Participants feeling lonely were more inclined to use social media to cope with lacking social contact.
items.explanation: Both claims independently find that loneliness leads to an increased inclination toward or actual usage of social media platforms.

items.a_text: Daily social networking site use of more than 2 hours is independently associated with poor self-rated mental health in children and adolescents.
items.b_text: In adjusted analyses, spending more than 3 hours per day on social media compared with no use is significantly associated with internalizing problems alone among adolescents.
items.explanation: Both claims independently demonstrate that spending substantial daily time on social media is significantly associated with adverse mental health outcomes in adolescents.

items.a_text: Greater overall social media use in adolescents is associated with higher levels of anxiety and depression.
items.b_text: For adolescent boys, anxiety triggers higher social networking site involvement.
items.explanation: Claim B provides a specific directional mechanism in adolescent boys that reinforces the positive association between social media use and anxiety identified in Claim A.

items.a_text: The decrease in adolescent psychological well-being may be at least partially due to the rapid adoption of smartphones and the subsequent shift in time use.
items.b_text: In the last decade, increasing mental distress and treatment for mental health conditions among youth in North America has paralleled a steep rise in the use of smartphones and social media by children and adolescents.
items.explanation: Both claims assert a consistent link between increased smartphone use and a rise in adolescent mental health issues or declining well-being.

items.a_text: Trimming and filling outlying studies reduces the random-effects pooled correlation estimate between social media use and depressive symptoms to r = 0.09.
items.b_text: Social media use of 5 or more hours daily retains an independent 11% higher depressive symptom score after adjusting for mediating factors.
items.explanation: Both claims independently demonstrate a positive association between social media use and depressive symptoms.

items.a_text: Individuals who use Facebook exhibit higher stress compared to non-users.
items.b_text: Facebook use affects well-being negatively.
items.explanation: Both claims independently indicate that Facebook use is associated with adverse psychological outcomes, specifically increased stress and reduced overall well-being.

items.a_text: Adolescents who spent more time on nonscreen activities were less likely to report mental health issues.
items.b_text: Adolescents aged 14 to 17 with high screen use (7+ hours per day vs 1 hour per day) are more than twice as likely to have taken medication for a psychological or behavioral issue in the last 12 months (RR 2.99).
items.explanation: Both claims provide mutually reinforcing findings that screen time is associated with poorer adolescent mental health outcomes, while non-screen activities are associated with fewer issues.

items.a_text: Parent and adolescent reports of adolescent social media account counts are moderately correlated with parent-reported DSM-5 symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, ODD, anxiety, and depression.
items.b_text: In adjusted analyses, spending more than 3 hours per day on social media compared with no use is significantly associated with comorbid internalizing and externalizing problems among adolescents.
items.explanation: Both claims provide mutually reinforcing evidence that greater adolescent social media involvement—measured either by account counts or time spent—is associated with increased internalizing and externalizing mental health problems.

items.a_text: Being female is significantly associated with addictive use of social media.
items.b_text: Female adolescents report significantly higher weekly time spent on social media than male adolescents.
items.explanation: Both claims independently indicate that female adolescents have significantly higher levels of social media engagement compared to males, whether measured by addictive use or time spent.

items.a_text: Adolescents who spent more time on nonscreen activities were less likely to report mental health issues.
items.b_text: Adolescents aged 14 to 17 with high screen use (7+ hours per day vs 1 hour per day) are more than twice as likely to have been treated by a mental health professional in the last 12 months (RR 2.22).
items.explanation: Both claims provide mutually reinforcing findings that greater engagement with non-screen activities is associated with better adolescent mental health, whereas high screen use is linked to increased mental health issues.
